item.title: You have a higher chance of getting cancer at a younger age than your parents. So what went wrong? | Devi Sridhar
item.description:
Some change in our lifestyles and environments over a generation has caused this increased risk. What, exactly, is a mystery

  • Prof Devi Sridhar is chair of global public health at the University of Edinburgh

In the field of global health, we often talk about each generation living longer and healthier lives than their parents. We’ve seen this in the gains in life expectancy, the sharp decrease in child mortality and in the near elimination of many vaccine-preventable diseases. But since the turn of the century this progress has stalled, and in some cases several health metrics have gone backwards.

Take cancer, which was long thought to be a disease linked to old age. While most cancers do indeed still occur in elderly people, a new report highlights that a number of cancers are increasing in people who are under 50, often referred to as “early onset cancer”. The report, undertaken by the World Cancer Research Fund, looked at data from 12 different cancer types in England, the US and the Netherlands over the past 20 years. What they found isn’t pretty.

Prof Devi Sridhar is chair of global public health at the University of Edinburgh

item.title: How do human beings rationalize genocide? NAZA provides a chilling look | Omer Bartov
item.description:
It’s easier to blame brutes and sadists for extreme violence. But as we see in the documentary, modern genocides are fueled by people who are uncomfortably recognizable

Werner Best, a senior SS official and jurist who helped organize the Nazi death squads that murdered hundreds of thousands of Jews, is also known for his statement: “We must destroy the enemy without hating him.” He belonged to a younger generation of Nazi technocrats, who despised the foul-mouthed, beer-bellied, brown-shirted “old fighters” of the Nazi party in the 1920s, and believed in organizing genocide neatly and dispassionately. After the fall of the regime, Best escaped justice for the rest of his long life, dying peacefully in Germany in 1989. His chilling statement came to my mind while I was watching the film NAZA.

I grew up in Tel Aviv and have visited there often in recent years. That is why the interviews with 24 Israeli soldiers and intelligence officers, which make up this documentary, felt strangely familiar. The conversations are conducted at night on rooftops, and the camera scans the cityscape, lingering on apartment windows as their inhabitants watch TV and make dinner. The landscape was intimately recognizable, and I felt a natural affinity with those people living their lives. I also recognized the way the interviewees talked – their speech patterns and choice of words. They reminded me of my son, who served more than a decade ago in the intelligence unit many of them might have belonged to.

item.title: ‘Like a drill going into my eye’: why the mystery over Havana syndrome refuses to die
item.description:
Dozens of CIA officers have been afflicted by debilitating symptoms over the past decade. Are they the result of ‘mass hysteria’? Or are they from attacks with an energy weapon and, if so, who is responsible? And has there been a cover-up?

Shortly after 1am one night in April 2019, a CIA officer on a work trip to London was jolted awake in his hotel room by the most intense head pain he had ever experienced. His body was soaked with sweat and he felt like his eyes were spinning in their sockets. He manoeuvred his way out of bed, hoping to make it to the bathroom to vomit, but found his sense of balance had deserted him. Eventually, he fell back into a fitful, shallow sleep.

The next day, arriving at the work meeting he had travelled for, the officer found he could not remember the names of colleagues in the room, people he knew well. As the meeting got under way, he could barely follow the discussion. Initially, he chalked it up to a terrible – if rather odd – case of food poisoning. But over subsequent weeks, worrying symptoms persisted: brain fog, loss of balance and increasingly harsh tinnitus.

item.title: Googlebooks mark the end of the old Google
item.description:
Does Google still believe in the open web? With the launch of its new Googlebooks, it doesn’t feel that way.

Googlebooks are Google’s attempt to establish a new platform of Android-based laptops, with native Android app support and tight connectivity with Android phones. They’re also an extension of Google’s efforts to rebuild Android around AI, with Gemini features just a quick cursor gesture away.

At the same time, Google plans to phase out ChromeOS, which it introduced in 2009 as a lightweight platform for the web. While Chromebooks remain popular in the education sector, Google says it will convert many existing models to Googlebooks, and it will end support for ChromeOS entirely by 2034.

it’s a sad end for what once represented Google at its most idealistic. Chromebooks weren’t just a breakthrough in speed and simplicity for laptops, they were also a bold bet on the open web as the next great computing platform. As the web becomes more walled off, and Google pivots to a platform more directly under its control, that dream has finally run its course.

How Chromebooks lost their way

The original goal for Chrome OS was to strip away all the overhead of a traditional laptop to make computing faster and easier. Here’s what Google wrote about the project in 2009:

“Speed, simplicity and security are the key aspects of Google Chrome OS. We’re designing the OS to be fast and lightweight, to start up and get you onto the web in a few seconds. The user interface is minimal to stay out of your way, and most of the user experience takes place on the web. And as we did for the Google Chrome browser, we are going back to the basics and completely redesigning the underlying security architecture of the OS so that users don’t have to deal with viruses, malware and security updates. It should just work.”

The first Chromebooks, which arrived in 2011, were basically just laptops that ran the Chrome browser, plus some extra window dressing. They had minimal internal storage and couldn’t run regular desktop software, but this allowed them to stay nimble, with speedy boot times, frictionless software updates, and minimal risk of malware. If a user lost their Chromebook, they could simply set up a new one and pick up where they left off.

In essence, Google was betting that nearly everything people did with their laptops would happen in a browser through sites like Gmail and Google Docs, so they could cut out all the other bloat to make those web apps shine.

To that end, Google encouraged app makers to build for the open web, with applications that could run in any browser, Chromebooks included. Although Google maintained a “Chrome Web Store” for web apps and extensions, the platform was only limited by the web itself. Anything you could run in a browser, you could run on a Chromebook, and that benefitted Google because it meant more people were using its search engine to find things.

“[A]ny time our users have a better computing experience [with Chrome OS], Google benefits as well by having happier users who are more likely to spend time on the Internet,” the company wrote in its 2008 blog post.

Over time, Google wavered on that original vision. It brought Android apps to Chrome OS in 2016, then added support for Linux apps in 2018. It even made a big foray into installable high-end gaming with Steam support.

While these inclusions made Chromebooks more capable, they also added new layers of complexity and demanded laptops with more storage. Setting up a new Chromebook became more of an ordeal, and preserving security became a bigger challenge. In shifting away from laptops powered by the open web, Chrome OS became exactly the kind of heavyweight computing experience it was trying to replace.

All this helped open the door for a new operating system built on Android instead. While Googlebooks will include a desktop-class version of Chrome, the emphasis now is on running Android apps and using AI.

Meanwhile, the original tenets of ChromeOS have disappeared. Look through Google’s announcement post for Googlebooks, and you will not find the words “speed,” “simplicity,” or “security” mentioned even once.

Times have changed, and so has Google

Google’s pivot away from a web-based operating system shouldn’t come as a major surprise. After all, Googlebooks are arriving at a time when the open web is destabilizing, in part because of Google itself.

Along with other tech companies that are all-in on AI, Google is betting on a world where browsing the web is increasingly unnecessary. Instead of using Google Search as a gateway to other sites, Google intends to have AI generate whatever information you need. Instead of managing your own email inbox, chatbots like Gemini will manage it for you. Instead of visiting websites to shop or make restaurant reservations, AI companies want to deploy fleets of AI agents to navigate those sites on your behalf.

As a result, using the web as a human is becoming more difficult. A growing number of websites are blocking themselves off from search engines and archival services in an attempt to keep AI crawlers out. Amazon has been limiting how many customer reviews some users can read because it thinks their behavior looks too robotic. Even just proving that you’re not a bot requires increasingly complicated steps, as in Google’s new ReCAPTCHA systems that demand phone-based verification or a recording of yourself performing hand gestures.

It’d be wrong to say that Google’s strategy with Chromebooks had anything to do with this. The company faltered on its original vision for a variety of other reasons, and the rise of AI would have been inevitable anyway.

Still, the arrival of Googlebooks serves as one final reminder of what we’ve lost. There was a time when Google believed in the open web more than anything, and it was committed to a platform with no real boundaries.

But that was back when getting folks to spend more time on the web was Google’s ultimate goal. Googlebooks exist for a world in which Google is clawing back more of that time for itself.

I grew up in France, where all children are taught about the revolutionary roots of their nation and what the state owes its citizens. The lessons leave their mark

Young British people have plenty to be angry about. Crushing student debt, private-school privilege, a housing market they can’t enter. Yet unlike their French counterparts, they have little tradition of turning that frustration into collective action. I grew up in France as a Briton, and for years I have watched my French friends do something my British ones never seem to: take to the streets.

“To arms, citizens! Form your battalions! Let’s march, let’s march!” It shouldn’t be too surprising, given the rousing lyrics of La Marseillaise, that France’s revolutionary spirit is not a relic of the past.

item.title: The more Putin escalates his attacks on Europe, the more Europe should support Ukraine | Timothy Garton Ash
item.description:
Moscow’s imperialist strongman believes decadent European democracies can be cowed. Our job is to prove him wrong

Vladimir Putin is escalating both his full-scale war against Ukraine and his shadow war against the rest of Europe. His main purpose in the shadow one is to break European support for Ukraine so he can subjugate that country, something he regards as existential for Russia’s future and his own. While we in the rest of Europe must prepare as best we can to defend ourselves against every kind of hybrid attack, the central thrust of our response should be to redouble our support for Ukraine. Ukraine is his main target. It’s there, and only there, not in a contest of a thousand hybrid pinpricks, that Putin’s Russia can in a meaningful sense be defeated and deterred.

In a powerful new book, Warum Russland nicht aufhören wird (Why Russia Won’t Stop), the German historian Martin Schulze Wessel shows how Putin’s policy fits into a much older Russian tradition of territorial expansionism and striving for hegemony, combined with a religiously infused imperial ideology. He reminds us that in 2016 Putin said “Russia’s frontier ends nowhere” and in 2025, “wherever the boot of a Russian soldier steps, that is ours”. West Europeans, fondly imagining that we have consigned such brute territorial imperialism to the dustbin of history, tend to think there must be some other explanation (eg something we did “wrong”, like the eastward expansion of Nato). Finns, Estonians and Poles know better. Despite Russia’s weaknesses, the author concludes, it is “the most dangerous country in the world”. Some in Asia might question that large claim, but certainly Russia is the most dangerous country for Europe.

item.title: Study explores links between 19th-century Manchester workers and enslaved Africans in Caribbean
item.description:
Global Threads research project reveals how slavery hung ‘like a spectre’ over the Peterloo massacre and other Mancunian struggles for equality

They were the killings that changed Britain, paving the way for working-class people’s right to vote, as well as leading to the founding of the Manchester Guardian. In the Peterloo massacre of 1819, peaceful protesters were shot and trampled to death by the Manchester and Salford Yeomanry at St Peter’s Field in the city.

A study by Global Threads, a public history project, has examined how the exploitation of Africans enslaved in the Caribbean was linked with the struggles of cotton workers at Peterloo. Though these workers were divided by thousands of miles and led different lives, they were exploited by the same forces – as Robert Wedderburn, a Black abolitionist in London, said at the time.

item.title: In three years, Israel's war on Gaza hasn't just changed the Middle East, it's changed the world | Steve Bloomfield
item.description:
A whirlpool of violence has engulfed everywhere from Lebanon to Yemen. Meanwhile, the west has destroyed any political authority it once had

There was a world before 7 October, 2023, and now there is a world after. For Gaza, for Israel, for the wider Middle East, and for everyone else too. Not all hinge points in history are obvious at the time. Three years on from the day it began, and precisely one year since a supposed ceasefire was agreed, this one is now impossible to ignore.

The before-and-after pictures tell part of the story. An update to Google Maps, released last week, underscores just what three years of relentless Israeli military onslaught has done to Gaza. Satellite images show how entire towns have been reduced to rubble. Mosques and hospitals, visible three years ago, have now disappeared. Meanwhile the once-empty shoreline is now crammed with tents. This is what it looks like when an attempt has been made to destroy a people.

Steve Bloomfield is the former international editor of the Observer

Author Natasha Lennard discusses how to disrupt the ‘certainties’ that don’t serve us and how to fight back

At the onset of the Covid pandemic in 2020, journalist Natasha Lennard started noticing a constant thrum of collective apprehension, epitomized in the phrase “in these uncertain times”. The expression acknowledged we didn’t have solutions for many of society’s problems: a globally spreading virus, the rise of the far right and stark “haves v have-nots” inequalities. In the years since, that “uncertainty” hasn’t gone anywhere, risking enabling paralysis – not knowing where to start to fix things and therefore giving up before trying.

In her new book, On Un/Certainty: The Uses of Doubt in Dangerous Times, Lennard, who also was an organizer in the 2011 Occupy Wall Street movement, deconstructs the problematic nature of giving in to uncertainty. She also uses the Austrian-British philosopher Ludwig Wittgenstein’s 1969 book On Certainty to question what is held as “certain” in today’s world, and who gets to make those calls.

item.title: I was kidnapped and held hostage for 977 days. Could I forgive my captors?
item.description:
At first the idea of mercy was something that helped me through the ordeal. But would real forgiveness be a form of Stockholm syndrome?

I knew Mohamed Tahlil as a gentle pirate who oversaw a team of guards during the first months of my life as a hostage in 2012. I had travelled to Somalia to report on the outbreak of modern piracy off the coast. On the 10th day, along a dusty road near Galkayo, in the centre of the country, I was kidnapped by pirates. For the next two and a half years, I was a hostage.

I spent most of my time on a thin, sweat-soaked foam mattress on the floor of a dusty room. The dim concrete prison houses changed, but the filth and the circumstances didn’t. Sometimes my captors moved me into the Somali savannah – where we camped in the open and slept on the ground – and for a six-month stretch, I was held on a hijacked tuna vessel, where I joined 28 fishers from east Asia who had been captured about three weeks before I was placed on board. (They had captured me on land, but they were a pirate gang, organised to capture ships at sea.) In each location, pirate guards would sit around with AK-47s and listen to the radio, or else chew khat, a narcotic plant.

item.title: Europe’s big election season is about to kick off. It could change everything | Nathalie Tocci
item.description:
If far right nationalists gain power in four big countries simultaneously, we are in for a dramatic Trumpian tilt

When it comes to Europe’s economy or its peace and security, it is obvious that decision-making has to be done largely at the European level to be meaningful. Yet electoral politics is still conducted mostly at the national level. The silver lining of this mismatch is that from country to country in Europe we have governments with different political priorities and leanings. Unlike in the US, where one presidential election can radically change the entire country’s course, as we have seen so vividly under Donald Trump’s leadership, the same drama has not so far unfolded in Europe. This may be about to change.

Pedro Sánchez rolled the dice in Spain last week, calling a snap election for next month after an unholy alliance of the conservative People’s party (PP), the far-right Vox and Catalan pro-independence party Junts blocked his big housing reform package in parliament. If the socialist prime minister, hailed by progressives globally but demonised by Europe’s right and Trump’s US, loses his election gamble, Spain could fall into the hands of a conservative/far-right coalition, which is currently ahead in the polls.

item.title: Former ARPA-H director Renee Wegrzyn wants to solve science’s ‘magic hands’ problem
item.description:
Renee Wegrzyn spent her career building the future of American science—including the Advanced Research Projects Agency for Health, or ARPA-H, the White House agency created to accelerate health breakthroughs.

Then the Trump administration showed her the door. Wegrzyn cofounded Transfyr to tackle what she calls one of the most overlooked issues in science: the magic hands problem. She explains why fixing this unglamorous bottleneck is the prerequisite for everything AI promises to deliver in medicine, and why she can feel the next Sputnik moment coming—even if she can’t quite name it yet.

This is an abridged transcript of an interview from Rapid Response, hosted by Robert Safian, former editor-in-chief of Fast Company. From the team behind the Masters of Scale podcast, Rapid Response features candid conversations with today’s top business leaders navigating real-time challenges. Subscribe to Rapid Response wherever you get your podcasts to ensure you never miss an episode.

You were at ARPA-H, the inaugural director of a White House effort to accelerate health research. You were amped up about the possibilities, but with the Trump administration, you had to pivot. Was it hard not to take it personally that they wanted different leadership?

I’ll tell you, I’m still amped up about it. It’s still an amazing idea. Obviously, DARPA [the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency] has been around for almost 80 years. I hope ARPA-H will have the same longevity and continue to live on today.

I’m a builder. I love to take things forward and really show what’s possible. So was it hard when I left? Of course it was hard. I had a really unusual appointment: I was a presidential appointee, but I was term-limited, so I served through the transition and had a few weeks in the new administration. I served in “Trump one,” by the way, as well.

So it was a great opportunity to make sure they really understood why we built the agency. We needed an ARPA-H because there was something missing in the way we were doing science broadly, which was: How do you move really quickly? How do you get focused on a problem versus building a general knowledge set? I was able to show them what we were building and convince them that it was worth keeping around. I couldn’t be more proud of the agency and its perseverance.

So your new business, Transfyr—The New York Times wrote about you, and the article kept referring to “magic hands.” I’m curious what magic hands are. What problem is Transfyr trying to solve or address?

You probably have your favorite dish, or your parents’ or grandparents’ favorite dish. Sometimes they just have the magic hands. Nobody can cook it like they do. Nobody can make it taste the special way they can. And that happens in science as well. There are some scientists who just have the knack and can deliver really great science over and over.

The challenge is that a lot of those scientists are such experts they can hardly describe what they’re doing. It’s an art in some ways. And so the magic hands idea was really a testament to what those scientists can do in the lab.

The pipeline we’re creating at Transfyr is: Can we create computer vision and perception tools to capture the work of science as it’s being done so that we understand, if the protocol says, “Mix the cells,” whether someone is inverting the tube in a certain gentle way, while another researcher may be rigorously shaking or vortexing it, which could destroy the sample?

Those little things, compounded over the many decisions a scientist may make over the course of several hours of experimentation, lead to what is called magic hands.

Was this an issue you saw at ARPA-H, the sort of breakthroughs that were trapped in a single lab in some ways?

Where that manifested at DARPA and at ARPA-H was in a realization, through my career, of how fragile breakthroughs are. Usually, the way a breakthrough is first communicated to the world is through a research publication, a Science or Nature paper. That paper is not a product. It’s not commercializable. It’s not ready for a patient that day. That’s the starting gun for what is going to happen.

The ARPAs of this world are really fantastic at getting to that initial breakthrough and demonstrating what is possible, but following through and delivering is not a 100% guaranteed activity.

When I started ARPA-H, we wanted customers, who would be the final users of that technology, to give us feedback on what we were developing so that when we got to the last day of the experiment, they were demanding that product, versus having that be the first contact with a customer, which unfortunately is pretty common around traditional grant-making organizations.

It’s rethinking how you make sure you can transfer that knowledge off the back end of a program.

Because the folks at the lab aren’t necessarily worrying about, or prioritizing, how to make it scalable. They’re just trying to see if it works. But of course, eventually we want it to be scalable.

Sometimes the folks in the lab don’t even have the expertise or understanding of who they need to talk to next to do that, right? We think about science and those transfers as handoffs. We deploy our technology to an originating lab to understand the science and what was important about that discovery, but we can also deploy it in a receiving lab so that we can see how they’re reproducing it.

And instead of the way we transfer science today, which is looking over each other’s shoulders and saying, “Oh, you’re doing it a little wrong,” we have this video-connectedness that lets us help accelerate those iterations of transferring the science.

Do you ever get frustrated about how resources are allocated in our world? You’ve put your life toward this work, and yet so much money is devoted to, I don’t know, space exploration or the next hot social app, the Meta Muse craze. How do you deal with government and how it prioritizes things?

Yeah, it’s maddening. One of the things that has me nervous right now is that I look back on the last 80 years following the Second World War. We’ve led the globe in science and engineering and innovation. Nobody who’s practicing science today has practiced science in the United States at a time when we weren’t, quote-unquote, winning from a competitiveness perspective, when we weren’t at the top.

I genuinely believe we may lose that competitiveness, that edge, that incumbency, and I’m not sure I see us fighting for it in the way that we should be. We have to deliver on what we’ve promised to do, and that’s a commitment not just to my country, but to my kids and my family. 

What I think a lot about is Sputnik moments. We’re going to look back at this moment in time like there’s something happening, and it’s going to impact whatever’s happening 20 to 50 years from now. You can feel it in the moment.

Where that happened before, of course, was Sputnik. The United States didn’t know the Soviet Union was developing that capability, and we didn’t have a counter-capability. What I realized is that each individual person has a Sputnik moment in their life that is usually health-related. My Sputnik moment was when my mother was diagnosed with cancer. That stopped everything.

Everybody has a story, whether it happened to them or their family, or if you talk to a member of Congress, something’s happening in their state that they can’t deal with.

So I’m like, “What is the Sputnik moment now?” If ARPA-H was bringing people from an unhealthy state to a healthy state, what’s happening now is taking us beyond that. If we can figure out and solve health and wellness, a lot of people talk about abundance. What is the next trajectory? What is the Sputnik that we’re working toward?

item.description:
After the executive’s failure to set a budget, and renewed culture-war confrontations, faith in the government’s ability to act in the common good is evaporating

Late last month, protesters deposited a sizable amount of foul-smelling green water on the steps of Stormont to draw attention to the appalling state of Lough Neagh, the largest freshwater lake in the British Isles. Years of agricultural pollution have created an environmental disaster in an area of huge ecological significance that once inspired the poetry of Seamus Heaney. Its plight should be a top priority for Northern Ireland’s devolved government. But the executive currently has other matters on its mind.

The sentencing of the former leader of the Democratic Unionist party (DUP) Jeffrey Donaldson, after he was convicted of child sexual abuse, dominated Thursday’s headlines. Meanwhile, a cross-party political crisis continues to play out. Halfway through the financial year, Stormont has yet to set a budget. The current deadlock in negotiations with the Northern Ireland secretary, Sir Chris Bryant, could lead to one being imposed from Westminster. Cuts are already being made by default amid an atmosphere of stasis and policy drift.

item.title: It’s not the old two-party politics – but Labour and the Tories now know they can shun their populist challengers | Gaby Hinsliff
item.description:
Though Burnham and Badenoch may still need the votes of Green and Reform supporters, both leaders have drawn clear lines in the sand

Ask a straight question, get a straight answer. It’s how politics is supposed to work but almost never does, which is why on the rare occasions it happens the result can be faintly chaotic. What did Andy Burnham mean when he said – in response to a question from the Tory MP Harriett Baldwin – that Labour couldn’t partner with the Green party while it remains wedded to the “Zionism is racism” motion its members have just endorsed? Were Green MPs now barred from a future coalition government? If so, what about councils where they are currently sharing power with Labour?

Though Burnham was only confirming what ministers have been arguing privately for days, at first nobody seemed to know: tellingly, it took almost 24 hours for the Labour party chair, Bridget Phillipson, to confirm that unless local Green groups disowned that idea sharpish, “Labour will bring any such local arrangement to an end”. So much for cuddly cross-party Andy, who always seemed so relaxed about rainbow coalitions. Now elected Greens in places such as Sheffield or Lewes must choose between power and members’ wrath, a useful rehearsal for what a hung parliament might feel like.

item.title: Dementia cases are expected to more than double by 2050. A new study reveals who’s most at risk
item.description:
More and more of our loved ones could develop dementia, as the number of diagnoses is projected to more than double by 2050, according to new research.

In the absence of large-scale prevention efforts, the number of people who are diagnosed with dementia each year could total 24.7 million by 2050, up from 11.4 million in 2023, according to a study by Australian researchers published in JAMA Psychology. Women and people who live in low- and middle-income countries already have higher rates of dementia, a trend that’s likely to continue, according to the findings.

While the researchers didn’t pinpoint an exact reason why dementia affects populations differently, they say the prospect of more cases warrants urgency in investing in prevention efforts. The prospect of 24 million new cases of dementia each year would place “enormous pressure on individuals, families, health systems and economies around the world,” Henry Brodaty, co-director of the Centre for Healthy Brain Ageing at the University of New South Wales Sydney and a co-author of the study, said in a statement.

“We cannot simply wait for people to develop dementia and then respond,” Brodaty said. “We need to act across the spectrum—from reducing modifiable risk factors and identifying people at risk earlier, through to improving diagnosis, treatment and care.”

The researchers studied data from more than 38,000 people diagnosed with dementia that span 18 countries or territories on six continents. They found that the incidence was somewhat higher among women—at 10.6 cases per 1,000 people versus 8.6 for men—but the difference was even starker depending on where people lived. The incidence of dementia was 13.6 cases per 1,000 people in low- and middle-income countries, compared with 8.3 in high-income countries.

Understanding the populations who are most at-risk for developing dementia will be key to developing prevention, diagnosis and care strategies, according to the study’s authors. 

“The higher incidence we observed in low- and middle-income countries is particularly concerning because these regions are experiencing rapid population aging while often having the fewest resources for prevention, diagnosis and care,” Perminder Sachdev, co-director of the Centre for Healthy Brain Ageing at the University of New South Wales in Sydney and a senior author of the study, said.

THE FINANCIAL TOLL OF DEMENTIA

Aging populations are understandably one of the main reasons why dementia cases are expected to increase, as this condition that affects memory, thinking and the ability to perform daily activities is more common after the age of 65. As of 2021, an estimated 57 million worldwide were living with dementia, according to figures from the World Health Organization, and it’s the seventh leading cause of death.

The World Health Organization likewise estimated that as of 2019, dementia cost economies around the world about $1.3 trillion, so a surge in new cases also carries a financial toll. 

That’s why the new research should sound an alarm, as Dr. Liron Sinvani, director of research and innovation at the Northwell Institute for Healthy Aging and professor at the Feinstein Institutes for Medical Research in New York, told U.S. News & World Report. “It’s an accelerating epidemic that demands immediate attention.” 

And that’s especially important as the countries that will face an “enormous wave” of dementia cases also have very limited infrastructure to respond, as Sinvani told the outlet. 

“Health systems must prepare for this massive increase in diagnostic and care demand, and this is especially true for these low- and middle-income countries where the growth will be fastest,” she said. “We know that dementia care requires a lot of caregiver support and is very costly. We will need a better infrastructure.”

Exclusive: Isabella Weber prescribes a common-sense solution to poverty, inequality and fascism – making life’s essentials affordable for all

The trouble with economists, Isabella Weber believes, is they do not behave like dentists. They obsess over ideological purity and are inflexible when searching for solutions, regardless of society’s symptoms. Dentists have no such pretensions – patients have little patience for dogma when in insufferable pain.

John Maynard Keynes, Weber clarifies in the canteen of the Wissenschaftskolleg zu Berlin (Berlin’s Institute for Advanced Study), was the first to draw this dental comparison – and she is running with it. As she sees it, the symptoms could not be more severe. “The status quo for the majority is entirely unbearable,” while extreme inequality and corporate concentration has reached levels “simply incompatible with democracy” worldwide. This is exacerbated by a climate crisis that “generates massive windfall profits” for big business as the “ecological foundations of our lives disintegrate”. All the while the far right is making hay.

item.title: How the quirky puffin became a symbol of the climate crisis – and hope
item.description:
In an extract from his new book, the nature historian explains how technology could help the seabird survive

For centuries human beings have exploited puffins, harvesting them by the thousand on their breeding grounds for their food and feathers. Over time, though, this relationship has changed, so that today we have come to love them, celebrating their quirky character and comical appearance and giving them a central place in our affections – a journey described by the environmental historian Dr Rob Lambert as the shift “from use to delight”.

How ironic, then, that just as we have come to truly appreciate them, our own existence now threatens theirs. The climate crisis threatens almost all the world’s roughly 11,000 species of birds, but its consequences have particularly dire significance for seabirds, whose life cycle is so intimately connected to the timing and abundance of their food supplies.

A modern-day prospector promised rural Imperial thousands of jobs and millions in tax revenue – but his plan has set off a firestorm of resistance

Sebastian Rucci zoomed in on a map in late 2024, looking closely at a large block of brown earth. The barren plot sandwiched between sprawling alfalfa fields and sleepy desert suburbs was exactly what he’d been searching for – the perfect place to realize his dream of building the largest artificial intelligence datacenter in California.

The dusty expanse wasn’t an obvious location. It was in the Sonoran desert, just north of the Mexican border, where temperatures regularly rose past 100F (37.8C). Water was scarce in the once-booming agricultural area, which gets its supply from the beleaguered Colorado River. And then, there was the city of Imperial – population 22,000 – to win over. As controversial datacenter projects have sprung up across the US, residents were naturally skeptical of a new, energy-guzzling neighbor.

item.title: The Climate Story Hiding in Plain Sight in the Global Economy
Hiding in plane sight: the invisible turbulence that can strike out of a clear blue sky
item.description:
As the planet warms, airlines are grappling with what this means for air travel – and for the passengers who simply refuse to keep their seatbelts fastened

It was a swelteringly hot afternoon in south-west Myanmar on 21 May 2024. Tropical thunderstorms, showers and highs of 36C were forecast for the area around the Irrawaddy Basin. High above, monsoonal heat and humidity were building into a vast convective column of water vapour, a towering cumulonimbus cloud soaring up to 35,000ft (more than 10,500 metres) into the air. From the ground, it would have looked like something from a children’s picture book – a soft, fluffy white mass. But for Singapore Airlines flight SQ321 passing just above, it was anything but benign.

In the cabin of the Boeing 777, passengers were being woken up for breakfast with three hours to go on the journey from London to Singapore. For the 210 travellers on board, the past 10 hours had been uneventful. The seatbelt signs were off. Some were milling around, others were using the toilets, and cabin staff were preparing trolleys for service. At 2.19pm and 23 seconds local time, moderate turbulence shook the plane for 17 seconds and the seatbelt sign was switched on. Then, as one passenger described it, it was “like a grenade had gone off”. In just 4.6 seconds, any passenger not strapped in hit the roof with 1.5 times the force of gravity and was thrown back on the floor in an instant.

Marco Rubio was once adamant that the US had to do everything in its power to end what he described as the “ethnic cleansing” of the Rohingya in Myanmar. In a 2017 letter he signed along with 20 other US senators, Rubio called for “strong multilateral sanctions against specific senior Burmese military officials associated with the gross human rights abuses”. Those responsible for the atrocities should be prosecuted, he argued.

In the years since, the Myanmar military’s crimes have only increased. What was then deemed ethnic cleansing of the Rohingya is now widely viewed, including by the US, as genocide. What little democracy existed in Myanmar was eradicated in 2021 when Aung San Suu Kyi was arrested and imprisoned and her party’s election victory overturned, and the military took full control.

item.title: Wikipedia often gets taken for granted – but its history is fascinating, and its future is fragile
item.description:
Wikipedia’s 68m articles have been consulted trillions of times. Not bad for a website that has barely changed since it was founded 20 years ago

A few years ago, I was struck by the tension between how Wikipedia was used, and how it was talked about. Everyone was on it all the time, and yet its reputation had stalled at “don’t trust it”, because it was the “free encyclopedia that anyone can edit”.

Clearly people were trusting it, so much so it had become part of the fabric of everyday life since it was founded by Jimmy Wales and Larry Sanger in 2001. But despite the fact it now has been consulted trillions of times by billions of people (English Wikipedia alone is 5.2bn words long), it inspires an odd lack of curiosity. Even people donating to Wikipedia might say the money was “for the factcheckers”, though there aren’t any – not paid ones, anyway. Meanwhile, the internet in the social media era had begun to feel like a much uglier place, and some digital nostalgia was setting in: here was this holdover that had somehow survived; a website that functions – and even looks – much the same as it did 20 years ago.

The show depicts prisons as places characterised by violence and isolation, with no focus on rehabilitation. It’s depressingly accurate

The new series of Time is not an easy watch. The opening seconds of Jimmy McGovern’s prison drama show a normal woman on a normal bus, as it drives up a normal road. But to the right of that road is a huge concrete wall, topped with barbed wire and CCTV cameras.

The wall is only partly visible, just as prisons themselves tend to occupy a space towards the very edges of our thoughts. They exist, but not as part of normal life. But McGovern’s drama shows just how permeable that wall is.

item.title: The problem with telling people the world is ending
item.description:
In the face of terrible crises, it can feel right to shock people into action. But what if that has the opposite effect?

These days, it’s easy to succumb to hopelessness. Whether you’re thinking about the climate crisis, the prospect of AI apocalypse, war or political turmoil, the list of challenges facing humanity can seem insurmountable.

It certainly feels unprecedented, and much of it may be. The sense of impending doom, on the other hand, is nothing new. And what we have learned from the past is that doomerism can lead to paralysis. If everyone freezes, then nothing changes – but if we want to have a chance of mitigating some of the threats I’ve mentioned then action is what’s required.
